newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-LEONARD WINS BATTLE OF YOUNG LIONS IN PGA OPENING ROUND.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEONARD WINS BATTLE OF YOUNG LIONS IN PGA OPENING ROUND.

text.p: Justin Leonard won the first day's battle among the young lions of golf at the PGA Championship, shooting two strokes better than Tiger Woods and Ernie Els, with some magical wedge work at Winged Foot Thursday.

British Open champion Leonard had the low round of the day's glamor grouping, a 68 that featured five par-saving, up-and-and downs from 50 yards out and longer -- the result of having to punch out of rough after errant drives.

"I spent quite a lot of time in the rough," said the 25- year-old Leonard, who joked that he did not require an afternoon workout due to a strenuous morning spent digging balls out of the thick junk lining the fairways.
"It was not a really pretty 68, but it sure looks good on the scorecard."
Leonard stood two strokes back of surprise early leader John Daly. His playing partners were also in the chase after shooting even-par 70s that could have been much better.

Masters champion Woods, 21, and U.S. Open winner Els, 27, also gave the huge galleries that followed the threesome much to cheer about as they both reached three under par on the front nine before fading.
Leonard said the key to his round was patience -- some sound advice he received Wednesday night from the legendary Byron Nelson, a fellow-Texan.
Woods, whose bid for the British Open was ruined by three horrendous holes, was undone once again by an adventure that produced a double-bogey seven on one of Winged Foot's two birdieable par-5s.
Els was felled by a double-bogey of his own -- when he tried to do too much from out of the rough at the eighth hole.
Woods wandered off course at the par-5 12th.

Standing 240 yards from the green after his drive at the 540-yard hole, Woods had to decide between hitting a soft 3-wood or a "nuked" 2-iron. He went with the 3-wood, eased up too much and shoved it out into trees on the right. He tried to punch out through an opening in the trees but popped the ball up into some branches and had to punch out again.

"The episodes I had at the British Open were just bad shots and you just can't afford to put the ball in gorse," said Woods, who posted a quadruple bogey and two triple-bogeys at Royal Troon. "I did something similar today. I put the ball in a tree and then I'm hitting two shots almost off my knees.
"You can't afford to hit the shots that far off line."
Els said he lost his composure after a tactical error.
"I really felt good about my round until I got to my tee shot on eight," he said. "I carved it into the trees and didn't have a very good lie. And I tried to get too cute with it.
"I tried to get it too far down the fairway and I hit it about eight yards. I really lost a lot of momentum there. I was quite angry at myself," admitted Els, who went on to bogey 10, 11 and 14.

Leonard avoided big mistakes, choosich out safely from the rough and rely on some fantastic wedge shots to save par -- from 60 yards to three feet at the fourth hole. From 103 yards to three feet at the 11th. From 80 yards to four feet at the 15th. From 50 yards out at both the 16th and 17th to within four feet and five feet.
The quiet Texan said he was steered straight by 85-year-old Byron Nelson, the guest of honor at a charity function Wednesday, who called him over for a word.
"He sat me down for a second, and he said, 'What do you think of the golf course?' And I told him what I thought. And he said, 'You know, I've played that golf course before.'

"'And when you hit it in the rough, just get it down there and get to where you've got an 8-iron or wedge or sand wedge in your hands. And you'll get a few up and down. And just avoid making big mistakes.
"I think I did precisely that today."
